clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant axonal (type 2) neuropathy caused by variants in GARS1, encoding glycyl-tRNA synthetase, notable for weakness and wasting that often begin in and predominate in the hands.

Upper-limb, hand-first onset with disproportionate involvement of the first dorsal interosseous and thenar muscles is a strong clue distinguishing CMT2D from most length-dependent, foot-first neuropathies.
It is allelic with distal hereditary motor neuropathy type V, so some family members show a pure motor picture with little or no sensory loss.
Sensory involvement, when present, is usually mild relative to the motor deficit, and reflexes may be reduced in affected limbs.
Nerve conduction studies reveal an axonal pattern with low motor amplitudes and near-normal velocities; the split-hand-like upper-limb emphasis can mislead towards a focal or motor neuron process.
Onset is typically in adolescence or early adult life, with slow progression, though phenotype and severity vary within families.
GARS1 is one of several aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase genes implicated in CMT, a mechanistic family that also includes YARS1, AARS1, HARS1 and others.
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating a pathogenic GARS1 variant, ideally with segregation across affected relatives given the dominant inheritance.
reference.pathophysiology: CMT2D is an autosomal dominant axonal peripheral neuropathy caused by heterozygous variants in GARS1, the gene encoding glycyl-tRNA synthetase, a housekeeping enzyme that charges transfer RNA with glycine during protein translation and functions as a homodimer in both the cytoplasm and mitochondria. Pathogenic variants are thought to act through a toxic gain-of-function or dominant-negative mechanism rather than simple loss of aminoacylation: mutant enzyme adopts aberrant conformations that expose neomorphic surfaces, mislocalises within the long axons of peripheral nerves, and interferes with axonal translation and neuropilin or other receptor interactions, producing a length-dependent yet strikingly upper-limb-predominant motor axonopathy. Because glycyl-tRNA synthetase is essential in every cell, the selective vulnerability of peripheral motor axons is attributed to their extreme length and high translational demand. GARS1 belongs to the family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase genes that cause dominant axonal CMT and distal hereditary motor neuropathy, and CMT2D is allelic with distal hereditary motor neuropathy type V, explaining the overlapping motor-predominant phenotypes seen across affected kindreds.
additionalDifferentials: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2C (TRPV4) with vocal cord and respiratory involvement
Distal hereditary motor neuropathy type V (allelic GARS1 phenotype)
Other aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase neuropathies (YARS1, AARS1, HARS1, WARS1)
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis or focal motor neuron disorders when hand wasting predominates
Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block
Hereditary neuralgic amyotrophy or a focal compressive upper-limb lesion
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and electromyography to confirm an axonal motor-predominant neuropathy with upper-limb emphasis
Targeted GARS1 sequencing or a hereditary neuropathy panel covering aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase genes
Detailed manual muscle testing documenting the hand-first, thenar and interosseous distribution
Sensory testing and sensory nerve action potential recordings to gauge the degree of sensory sparing
Antibody and immunological work-up to exclude multifocal motor neuropathy where the picture is atypical
Family history construction and segregation testing of at-risk relatives
Neuromuscular imaging or ultrasound where needed to characterise the pattern of muscle involvement
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or asymmetric weakness prompting reassessment for motor neuron disease or an acquired cause
Prominent upper motor neuron signs, which are not expected and suggest an alternative diagnosis
Significant sensory loss out of keeping with the usually motor-predominant phenotype
New bulbar or respiratory symptoms warranting urgent evaluation
Sudden functional decline in hand use affecting safety and independence
reference.prognosis: CMT2D usually progresses slowly, with hand and later foot weakness causing variable disability; most patients retain ambulation, though marked intrinsic hand-muscle wasting can substantially impair fine motor function. Severity and rate of progression differ between and within families.
pitfalls: Expecting the classic foot-first pattern and dismissing a hand-onset presentation as non-neuropathic
Confusing the upper-limb-predominant wasting with a focal entrapment or split-hand of motor neuron disease
Assuming prominent sensory loss must be present, when sensory features are often mild or absent
Testing only PMP22 or common CMT1 genes and missing the synthetase group
Overlooking affected relatives with a pure distal motor neuropathy phenotype during family assessment
references: Clinical review of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase neuropathies
management: No disease-modifying therapy; supportive and rehabilitative care through a neuromuscular multidisciplinary team
Occupational and hand therapy with splints and adaptive aids for the intrinsic hand-muscle wasting and fine-motor loss that dominate early
Physiotherapy and ankle-foot orthoses for later length-dependent lower-limb weakness and foot drop
Neuropathic pain management where sensory symptoms are present
Avoidance of neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine
Autosomal dominant genetic counselling with segregation testing of at-risk relatives
Regular neuromuscular clinic follow-up to track progression and functional needs
